questions.q: How does David say Yahweh will protect him?
questions.a: Yahweh equips David to fight well in wars.

questions.q: What does David say Yahweh does for him?
questions.a: David says Yahweh keeps him safe and helps him escape from danger and enables him to rule people under him.

questions.q: What does David think about Yahweh’s attention to people?
questions.a: David finds it amazing that Yahweh pays any attention to people, since they are so insignificant.

questions.q: To what does David compare people’s lives?
questions.a: David says people live only a short time just as a mist or a shadow quickly disappears.

questions.q: What would the mountains do if Yahweh touched them?
questions.a: Yahweh would cause the mountains to smoke if he touched them.

questions.q: What does David ask Yahweh to send against his enemies?
questions.a: David asks Yahweh to send lightning bolts to send his enemies running.

questions.q: How does Yahweh rescue David from the power of foreigners?
questions.a: Yahweh reaches down from heaven and rescues David from the power of these foreign enemies.

questions.q: On what instrument will David sing a new song to God?
questions.a: David will sing a new song to God and praise him with a lyre which is a harp with ten strings.

questions.q: What does David say God does for kings and for him?
questions.a: David says God saves kings and rescues him from danger in battle.

questions.q: What do the mouths of the foreigners speak?
questions.a: Their speak things that are not true and swear false oaths.

questions.q: What does David want the sons of the Israelites to be like?
questions.a: He wants them to be strong like plants that grow to full size in their youth.

questions.q: What does David want the daughters of the Israelites to be like?
questions.a: He wants them to be as beautiful and stately as pillars that craftsmen carve to decorate a palace.

questions.q: What does David ask God to provide?
questions.a: David asks that the barns be full of many kinds of crops and that the flocks multiply greatly in the fields.

questions.q: What does David ask God to spare the nation from?
questions.a: David asks that there would be no enemies who could break through their walls, no one going into exile, and no crying out in distress in the city squares.

questions.q: Who does David say are the people who are happy?
questions.a: He says those who worship Yahweh as their God will be happy and have a good life.

commentary.text: David acknowledges the great goodness of God, and prays for help.
He prays for the prosperity of his kingdom.

Verses 1–8 When men become eminent for things as to which they have had few advantages, they should be more deeply sensible that God has been their Teacher. Happy those to whom the Lord gives that noblest victory, conquest and dominion over their own spirits. A prayer for further mercy is fitly begun with a thanksgiving for former mercy. There was a special power of God, inclining the people of Israel to be subject to David; it was typical of the bringing souls into subjection to the Lord Jesus. Man's days have little substance, considering how many thoughts and cares of a never-dying soul are employed about a poor dying body. Man's life is as a shadow that passes away. In their highest earthly exaltation, believers will recollect how mean, sinful, and vile they are in themselves; thus they will be preserved from self-importance and presumption. God's time to help his people is, when they are sinking, and all other helps fail.

Fresh favours call for fresh returns of thanks; we must praise God for the mercies we hope for by his promise, as well as those we have received by his providence. To be saved from the hurtful sword, or from wasting sickness, without deliverance from the dominion of sin and the wrath to come, is but a small advantage. The public prosperity David desired for his people, is stated. It adds much to the comfort and happiness of parents in this world, to see their children likely to do well. To see them as plants, not as weeds, not as thorns; to see them as plants growing, not withered and blasted; to see them likely to bring forth fruit unto God in their day; to see them in their youth growing strong in the Spirit. Plenty is to be desired, that we may be thankful to God, generous to our friends, and charitable to the poor; otherwise, what profit is it to have our garners full? Also, uninterrupted peace. War brings abundance of mischiefs, whether it be to attack others or to defend ourselves. And in proportion as we do not adhere to the worship and service of God, we cease to be a happy people. The subjects of the Saviour, the Son of David, share the blessings of his authority and victories, and are happy because they have the Lord for their God.
